title: Chapter 5.6 — Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

cards.back: An inequality that can be written in one of these forms: $ ax + by < c $, $ ax + by \le c $, $ ax + by > c $, or $ ax + by \ge c $, where $ a $, $ b $, and $ c $ are real numbers.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:linear inequality in two variables]]?
What is a [[kw:solution of a linear inequality in two variables]]?
cards.back: An ordered pair $(x, y)$ that makes the inequality true when substituted for $x$ and $y$.
Substitute the $x$ and $y$ values into the inequality. Simplify. If the resulting statement is true, it is a solution. If false, it is not.
cards.front: How do you check if an ordered pair is a solution of a linear inequality?
What is the first step in graphing a linear inequality in two variables?
cards.back: Graph the [[imp:boundary line]]. Use a dashed line for $<$ or $>$. Use a solid line for $\le$ or $\ge$.

cards.front: When do you use a dashed boundary line?
cards.back: When the inequality symbol is strict: $<$ or $>$. Points on the line are [[imp:not solutions]].

cards.front: When do you use a solid boundary line?
cards.back: When the inequality symbol includes equality: $\le$ or $\ge$. Points on the line [[imp:are solutions]].

cards.front: What is the purpose of a test point when graphing an inequality?
cards.back: To determine [[imp:which side of the boundary line]] to shade. If the test point satisfies the inequality, shade that side. If not, shade the other side.

cards.front: Why is $(0, 0)$ often used as a test point?
cards.back: Because it makes calculations easy. However, it cannot be used if the boundary line passes through the origin.
Draw a solid horizontal line at $y = 2$. Test $(0,0)$: $0 \le 2$ is true. Shade the [[imp:half-plane below]] the line.
Rewrite as $y > \frac{1}{2}x + 1$. Draw a dashed line. Test $(0,0)$: $0 > 1$ is false. Shade the half-plane [[imp:above]] the line (the side not containing the origin).
[[imp:All solutions]] of the inequality. Every point in the shaded region makes the inequality true.
cards.front: What does the shaded region of a linear inequality represent?
You can spend at most $10 on grapes ($2.50/lb) and apples ($1/lb). Write the inequality.
cards.back: Let $x$ = pounds of grapes, $y$ = pounds of apples. $$2.5x + y \le 10$$

cards.front: In the fruit salad problem, why do we only graph in the first quadrant?
cards.back: Because the amounts of fruit cannot be negative. The variables represent [[imp:non-negative quantities]].
